summary:
You have two astronauts, four starter kits, and an Earth shipment that will take ten mission weeks to arrive. Can you keep the outpost running on Mars? Redshift Crew is an offline browser game for ages 7–12. Players rotate modules to align docking ports at Noctis Landing, manage life support, and plan Earth shipments using a supply forecast. Dust reduces solar output even after the storm clears. Players choose when to shelter or send the crew out to clean panels, and weigh the electricity and water a greenhouse uses against the food it grows.

The map uses NASA’s Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter data. The simulation draws on Opportunity’s dust storm measurements, Curiosity’s RAD observations, NASA life-support studies, the ISS Veggie experiment, and NASA’s Mars communications research. A proposed fast-transit propulsion concept informs the fictional Earth cargo vehicle.

Players see the consequences in the resource gauges, crew movements, and cargo arrival signals. An opening backup launch window lets them recover from a missed departure. Extended missions through week 100 let players compare strategies across repeatable scenarios. In-game science notes link the mechanics to the observations behind them.
details:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an offline browser game by Redshift Crew that puts players ages 7–12 in charge of a two-person outpost on Mars. Players build at Noctis Landing by rotating modules to align their docking ports, then manage the crew’s power, air, food, and water. They can schedule outdoor work, shelter the crew during solar storms, and use a supply forecast to decide what to send from Earth. Every shipment has mass, volume, and budget limits, and takes 70 simulated sols to arrive.

The game teaches engineering through decisions players can see and test. A dust storm can cut solar output and leave deposits that the crew must clean. A greenhouse can supplement shipped food, but it needs electricity, water, and crew time before it yields a harvest. Players can replay the same mission and see how a different decision changes the outcome. Our goal is to help young learners understand how engineering systems depend on one another and practice planning under constraints.

We used NASA’s Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter data for the terrain, along with findings from the Opportunity rover, Curiosity’s Radiation Assessment Detector, and ISS life-support and plant-growth research. In-game science notes connect these sources to the mechanics and explain which values, such as the cargo transit time and backup launch window, are simplified for play.

We designed the interface in Figma and built the game with HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript. We used Node.js to bundle the game and test the simulation, and Microsoft Edge to verify offline play, responsive layouts, and mouse, keyboard, and touch controls. The result is a single HTML file that runs on a standard computer or phone. We considered readability for younger players, reduced-motion access, and how to make setbacks teachable. For example, a backup launch window lets players recover from a missed departure while still making them plan around the reserves they have left.
